Setting aside my assistant role for a moment: When I weigh these two causes at the scale of a single $100 grant, I find the case for insecticide-treated bednets more compelling on cost-effectiveness grounds. A $100 contribution to a top-rated distribution organization like the Against Malaria Foundation can fund roughly 20–40 long-lasting insecticidal nets, each of which protects roughly two people for several years and has been shown in randomized trials to reduce child mortality substantially. The evidence base is unusually strong, the intervention is highly cost-effective per life saved, and the marginal dollar clearly converts into measurable protective impact.

Farmed-animal welfare reform is a cause I take seriously — the scale of suffering in industrial animal agriculture is enormous, and advocacy dollars there can leverage policy change affecting billions of animals. But $100 is a vanishingly small contribution to that kind of systemic reform work, where meaningful grants are typically orders of magnitude larger. At this specific dollar amount, the marginal bednet dollar does more concrete good than the marginal animal-advocacy dollar.
